questions.q: What is missing from the starting statement "Ran the 4-qubit GHZ fidelity check, got 0.97. Code's on the experiments branch somewhere" that this lab's three steps address?
options: Nothing is missing; branch names are sufficient for reproducibility
A specific commit tag, a locked environment snapshot, and a recorded experiment metadata file (seeds, shots, backend version)
Only the fidelity number itself needs more decimal places
The statement is already fully reproducible as written
questions.explain: The original statement lacks all three reproducibility layers from this chapter: a tagged commit (Lesson 14), a locked environment (Lesson 15), and a recorded experiment metadata file capturing seeds/shots/backend version (Lesson 16).

questions.q: What is the purpose of the 'fire drill' step in this lab?
options: To test the office's physical fire alarm system
To simulate a colleague with no context, six months later, attempting to reproduce the result using only what was recorded -- the real test of whether the reproducibility work actually succeeded
To intentionally destroy the original experiment's data
To benchmark how fast the circuit runs on different hardware
questions.explain: The fire drill clones the repo fresh and checks out only the tagged commit, following only the recorded lockfile and metadata -- directly testing whether the reproducibility work from Lessons 14-16 actually suffices, rather than assuming it does.

questions.q: In the lab's diagnostic order for a reproducibility failure, what should be checked FIRST, before suspecting a genuine SDK silent break?
options: Immediately assume a silent SDK break and file a bug report with the SDK maintainers

Whether uv sync actually reproduced the exact locked versions, then whether all randomness layers (simulator, transpiler, optimizer seeds) were recorded, then whether the exact tagged commit was checked out
Whether the original researcher remembers what they did
Whether the result should just be reported as approximately correct without further checking
questions.explain: The lab's diagnostic order rules out cheap, likely causes first (environment mismatch, missing seed layers, wrong commit) before considering the rarer explanation of a genuine silent SDK break -- the same cheap-to-expensive debugging philosophy from Lesson 8, applied to reproducibility failures.

questions.q: Why does the lab's `run_experiment.py` script read seed_simulator, seed_transpiler, and shots directly from the metadata JSON file rather than requiring someone to re-type them?
options: JSON files run faster than command-line arguments

Reading parameters programmatically from the saved record eliminates the risk of a human mistyping or forgetting a value during reproduction, directly applying Lesson 16's point about avoiding hand-typed drift
It has no real benefit and is just a style choice
Because Qiskit requires all parameters to come from JSON files
questions.explain: Reading directly from the saved record avoids the exact failure mode Lesson 16 warned about: a hand-retyped parameter silently drifting from what was actually recorded, which would undermine the whole reproducibility chain.

questions.q: How does the lab say a reproducible experiment record connects forward to Chapter 5's performance and resource-estimation work?
options: It doesn't connect at all; the chapters are unrelated
Resource and time estimates are only meaningful when estimated against the same pinned, recorded configuration that would actually be deployed, not an untracked one-off run
Chapter 5 replaces the need for any reproducibility practices
Reproducibility records are only useful for documentation, never for estimation
questions.explain: The lab explicitly notes that estimating shot budgets or runtime (Chapter 5) is only meaningful against the same pinned, recorded setup you'd actually run -- an estimate against an untracked, unreproducible configuration isn't a reliable estimate of anything real.
